Probate1848 forward
Marriage records1885 forward
Criminal1995 forward
PlatsAvailable on the stations

The office occupies the first floor at 155 North Cass Street, Centerville, TX 75833. The clerk's page spells out a few house rules for visitors:

  • No photographs of the large Tobin maps or of images on the public stations, and no flash photography.
  • Carrying a document, page or volume out of the office is a state jail felony (Penal Code 32.47).
  • Staff give no legal advice, do not decide who owns surface or mineral rights, and do not run lien searches.
  • Attorney General Opinion WW-607 is cited for the point that the clerk has no duty to search the records and vouch for them.

When does the Leon County Clerk stop taking documents, and what does recording cost?

The office runs 7:45 a.m. to 4:45 p.m. each weekday without a lunch closure, yet recording itself ends at 4 p.m. Whatever arrives after that goes onto the next business day's work. The office takes cash, checks and major credit cards.

The posted charge is $15 for page one of an instrument and $4 for each page after it, under a schedule the office says began on January 1, 2024. Electronic filing into the official records runs through three named vendors, Simplifile, CSC and ePN. Fees shift over time, so verify the amount with the clerk's staff first.

Different deputies take different work. General recording, indexing and copy requests sit with the chief deputy, while probate, civil filings, marriage licenses and vital records each have their own staff member and phone menu option, so say at the start of a call that you are asking about recording a deed. The page also reminds visitors that clerks are not attorneys and cannot say what needs to be filed.

What does Texas require before a Leon County deed can be recorded?

A land conveyance may be recorded only after the owner signs it and swears to it or acknowledges it, either before two witnesses or before an officer such as a notary, county clerk, district clerk or county court judge (Property Code 12.001(b)).

The 2023 county clerk manual describes the instruments that land in deed records: general and special warranty deeds, quitclaims, trustee's deeds, sheriff's deeds and tax deeds, plus lien releases, affidavits and contracts of sale. Its statutory base is $5.00 for page one and $4.00 for later pages, with other clerk charges added, and leaving off the grantee's mailing address can add $25. For an actual filing, use the figure Leon County posts.

Nobody can go back and write new heirs into an old deed. After an owner's death, the manual points to an executor's or administrator's deed for an administered estate, a court order with the will for a muniment of title, or an affidavit of heirship when nothing else is available.

What is Leon County like for a homeowner or seller?

Leon County is rural, east of Waco on Interstate 45 between Dallas and Houston. Census estimates for July 2025 count 16,894 people, up 7.2 percent since 2020. Within 1,073.16 square miles of land are 9,255 housing units and 6,741 households.

Survey results for 2020 through 2024 list 76.6 percent owner occupancy and a middle owned-home value of $186,400. Monthly housing costs for owners with a mortgage sit at $1,557, those without a mortgage pay $502, and rent runs $907. Commutes average 29.3 minutes, and 27.9 percent of the population is 65 or older.

According to the Handbook of Texas, the county was carved from Robertson County in 1846. Leona served first as seat of government, and Centerville took over in 1851. Buffalo is the biggest community, and Jewett, Normangee, Oakwood and Marquez are also named. U.S. 79 crosses east to west, the Trinity River marks the eastern edge, and Lake Limestone fills part of the northwest corner. Oil and gas, agribusiness and lumber anchor the economy.

Who handles Leon County values and tax bills?

The Leon Central Appraisal District sets values and the county tax assessor-collector issues bills. The county's page directs owners with account changes or value questions to the appraisal district at 141 W. St. Mary's, Centerville, TX 75833, telephone 903-536-2252.

That page also names the firms that chase delinquent accounts for each unit. One Waco firm covers the county, a Corsicana firm covers Normangee ISD, and a Tyler firm covers Buffalo ISD, the City of Marquez and Oakwood ISD. If a collection letter shows up, the unit that sent it tells you which firm to contact.

Statewide, values freeze as of January 1, bills show up in October, and penalty-free payment ends January 31. A tax lien takes hold every January 1, so a Leon County house enters any sale still owing that year's tax. Our Leon County property tax guide covers the tax office itself.

What title problems turn up in the Leon County records?

The commonest one is an estate nobody opened. Where 27.9 percent of people are 65 or older, a parent's name often stays as the last owner of record, and the file then needs a legal path to the heirs.

  • Four years from the date of death is the usual window to probate a will, and a judge may take a late filing for an acceptable reason.
  • A small estate affidavit needs no will, no pending administration, assets up to $75,000 apart from homestead and exempt property, and every heir's agreement. Two disinterested witnesses swear to it, and the death must be at least 30 days old.
  • A muniment of title lets a will serve as proof of ownership when the only debts are real estate liens.
  • Heirs can file a sworn heirship statement with the Leon County Clerk, though nothing obliges a buyer or lender to rely on it.

Heirs seeking a homestead exemption without being named on a recorded deed supply the appraisal district with a sworn statement of their interest, a death certificate and a current utility bill.

Can I sell a Leon County house with a title or lien problem?

Yes. A cash buyer can accept the house exactly as it is, with the closing agent settling recorded items wherever a payoff is documented. If you found an unreleased mortgage, a probate gap or a back tax bill in the Leon County records, send us the details and we will outline the likely route to closing.

More questions about Leon County, TX Property Records

What is the last hour to file a document in Leon County?

At 4 p.m., although the office stays open until 4:45 p.m. on weekdays. Papers that arrive later are handled the following business day.

What fee applies to filing a deed with the Leon County Clerk?

Search the clerk's foreclosure sales portal and the Official Public Records for a notice of trustee sale. Sales take place on the first Tuesday of each month, so a notice on file points to the next first Tuesday. A title company can confirm the status.

Bell County by the numbers

Where do I search and record property records in Bell County?

Deeds, liens and plats for Bell County are filed with the County Clerk in Belton, and the Property Records/Recordings desk answers at (254) 933-5171. The clerk works from the Bell County Justice Center at 1201 Huey Road, Belton, TX 76513, weekdays from 8 in the morning to 5 in the afternoon, and takes mail at P.O. Box 480 in Belton.

The clerk's real estate page says the Official Public Records are searchable online, and the main clerk page also links a SUPERSEARCH tool that uses OCR plus a CountyFusion search. A Property Fraud Alert sign-up sits on the same page, which is worth a few minutes if you own a house you rarely visit.

Plan around the cutoff. The clerk takes no daily business transactions after 4:30 p.m., and the cutoff moves to 4:15 p.m. on the last business day of the month. If you are closing on a month-end Friday, get the signed original to the title company early.

  • Recording desk: (254) 933-5171, with an email address listed for deed recordings on the clerk's page
  • Civil and probate records: (254) 933-5174
  • Plats: an alphabetical and numerical directory on the clerk's site
  • Mailed recordings: Attn: Recording Dept., P.O. Box 480, Belton

What will Bell County charge to file a deed?

Filing a single-page deed in Bell County costs $10.00, made up of a $5.00 filing fee and a $5.00 records management fee. Each added page that carries visible marks is $4.00, and the clerk adds $0.25 for each grantor or grantee indexed past the first five. The schedule below is the clerk's own, listed as effective January 1, 2024 after Senate Bill 1612.

The clerk also prints a page-count chart. These totals come straight from it:

  • 1 page: $10.00

The office states it cannot hold or record an instrument without the proper fee, and it does not accept personal out-of-state checks.

What must a document show before the Bell County Clerk accepts it?

It must be an original, notarized document or a certified copy of the original. The clerk's page also asks filers to leave a 2 inch margin for the recording stamp and instrument number.

State law backs up the notary step. A conveyance of real property can be recorded only if it is signed and acknowledged, or sworn to, before an authorized officer, according to the Texas county clerk manual. The same manual says a deed that leaves out a grantee's mailing address can pick up an extra $25 charge, so check that line before you sign.

Electronic filing is limited to the entities named in Local Government Code 195.003, such as attorneys, banks and title companies. Bell County lists these e-recording vendors: CSC, EPN eRecording Network, Simplifile, Hopdox and Indecomm Global Services. A homeowner mailing a deed to the clerk, by contrast, sends the paper original.

How is Bell County laid out, and what does that mean for a records search?

Bell County is a 1,055 square mile county in east central Texas, roughly 45 miles north of Austin, and its records cover very different kinds of land. The Handbook of Texas describes the Balcones Escarpment running through the middle, with level Blackland Prairie farmland to the east and rolling Grand Prairie uplands to the west.

The county was formed in 1850 and its seat, first called Nolanville, took the name Belton in 1851. Today Killeen is the largest city, and Temple grew up around the Santa Fe railroad headquarters in 1881. Other towns include Harker Heights, Nolanville, Salado and Morgan's Point Resort. Interstate 35 and U.S. 190 are the main roads, and Belton Lake and Stillhouse Hollow Lake shape the lakeside lots.

That mix produces the paperwork variety a title searcher sees here: old farm tracts with metes and bounds descriptions, subdivision plats around Killeen and Temple, lakefront parcels, and homes near Fort Cavazos, the military post in the western part of the county.

Census Bureau QuickFacts supplies these numbers:

  • Mid-2025 estimate: 402,248 residents, 8.5 percent above the 2020 base
  • Housing units: 165,094, of which 56.5 percent are lived in by their owners
  • Typical owned home, 2020 to 2024 survey: valued at $241,000
  • Typical monthly rent: $1,224
  • Veterans in the county: 48,220

Who sets the value of a Bell County property?

The Bell Central Appraisal District sets value, and the clerk only records the deed. The district keeps three public offices: Belton at 411 E. Central (254-939-5841), Killeen at 301 Priest Dr. (254-634-9752) and Temple at 205 E. Central (254-771-1108). All three open weekdays until 4:45 p.m., and one mailing box, P.O. Box 390 in Belton, serves them.

Its contact page sends deed and address-change questions to a mapping email, which matters after a sale: a recorded deed is what lets the district update ownership. Protests have their own address, and the district says protests will not be accepted at any other inbox.

Appraisals reflect ownership and condition on each January 1, with homestead notices mailed around April 1. A protest is due May 15 or 30 days from delivery of the notice, whichever falls later. Schools exempt $140,000 of a homestead's value, and owners aged 65 and up or with a disability get another $60,000.

How do Bell County records affect a house sale?

Whatever is recorded against the house shows up in the title search and can delay closing until it is paid or released. The Comptroller explains that each year's tax lien attaches January 1, and whoever owned the house on that day stays liable for that bill even after selling.

Foreclosure is visible in the same records. Trustees post a sale notice at the courthouse and file a copy with the clerk 21 or more days ahead, and the auction runs the first Tuesday of the month from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Bell County's schedule lists foreclosure postings at $2.00 when the trustee does it and $12.00 when the clerk posts.

Inherited houses add another layer. The State Law Library describes an affidavit of heirship as a sworn statement placed on file with the clerk, and nothing obliges a buyer or lender to rely on it. A deed that transfers property at death has to be recorded while the owner is alive, and a muniment of title order and will go to the clerk where the land lies.

  • Unpaid taxes, old mortgages and judgments need payoff letters before closing
  • Missing heirs or an unprobated will can stop a title company from insuring
  • A plat or survey mismatch is fixed by a corrective instrument that gets recorded

What will Bell County charge to file a single-page deed?

The charge is $10.00, split into a $5.00 filing fee and a $5.00 records management fee. Each added page with visible marks is $4.00, and names indexed beyond five are $0.25 each.

Is electronic filing open to homeowners in Bell County?

Only qualified filers can e-record. Local Government Code 195.003 limits it to groups such as attorneys, banks and title companies, working through vendors the clerk names. A homeowner mails or hand-delivers the notarized original in Belton.

When does the Bell County Clerk stop taking recordings each day?

Daily business transactions end at 4:30 p.m., and 4:15 p.m. applies on the last business day of the month, so month-end closings need documents delivered ahead of time.

Where can I order a certified Bell County deed copy?

Ask the County Clerk's recording desk at (254) 933-5171. The posted rate for a certified copy is $1.00 plus $1.00 per page, and a plain copy is $1.00 per page.

Which office handles questions about my Bell County valuation?

The Bell Central Appraisal District does. Its Belton line is 254-939-5841, Killeen is 254-634-9752 and Temple is 254-771-1108.

Mclennan County by the numbers

Where do I find McLennan County property records?

The McLennan County Clerk keeps the county's deed records in Waco, on the second floor of the Records Building at 215 N 5th Street, Room 223. Call 254-757-5078 to reach the counter, which opens on weekdays from 8 a.m. until 5 p.m. and closes on county holidays.

The same office also holds liens, hospital liens, cattle brands, assumed name certificates and marriage licenses, and it clerks the probate court and the commissioners' court. For a seller, one counter therefore holds most of what a title company asks for. Staff will not interpret a document, so legal questions go to an attorney or a legal aid group.

In Texas the county clerk doubles as county recorder, and a deed is filed where the land lies. A house anywhere in McLennan County is recorded in this office, wherever its owner lives.

How far back do the McLennan County records go?

Clerk records begin in 1849 and continue to the present, divided between bound volumes and an electronic system. Anything recorded on or after January 1, 1996 can be searched online or on public workstations in the clerk's office, the county says.

The middle rows overlap because the county lists its older material in more than one place. For a deed recorded before 1996, phone the clerk first and ask which format holds it.

How do I search the McLennan County records?

Search by name. McLennan County does not index by legal description, the clerk says, so you need the grantor or the grantee, which means the seller or the buyer named on the deed.

  • The Online Records Search, linked from the clerk's Official Public Records page, covers everything recorded since 1996.
  • The public workstations in the Records Building cover older volumes and anything the online tool leaves out.
  • A survey is unlikely to turn up. Surveys are not recordable by themselves in Texas, so the county has one only when it rode along as an exhibit to another document, which seldom happens.

Note the volume and page or the instrument number of each document you locate, so the title company can order exact copies instead of searching again.

What does McLennan County require to record a deed?

The clerk posts a short list of filing standards, and a document that misses one comes back unrecorded. The office adds that it will record only finished documents that meet those standards and cannot advise on legal matters.

  • The land must lie in McLennan County, and any real property document needs a legal description.
  • Signatures must be originals, proved, acknowledged or sworn to as Texas law requires.
  • Only originals are accepted, apart from certified copies issued by another government agency.
  • It needs a heading naming its type, must be written in English, and must show a return address.
  • A deed also needs the grantee's address, which the clerk says serves tax purposes.
  • Payment options: cash, cashier's or business checks, money orders, personal checks, and Visa, MasterCard or American Express.

Two practical points come from the clerk's FAQ. Nobody at the counter can notarize your signature, so get the deed acknowledged beforehand, and the recorded original goes back by mail the next business day.

What does it cost to record a deed in McLennan County?

The Texas Courts county clerk manual describes the statutory base: $5.00 for page one, $4.00 for each additional page, and $0.25 per name beyond five that has to be indexed. Add-on fees include up to $10 for records management, up to $10 for a records archive and $2.00 for technology.

Leaving the grantee's mailing address off a deed can add $25. The county posts its own Recording Fee Schedule as a PDF on the Official Public Records page, so rely on that for the exact total and confirm it with the clerk or title company before you write a check.

What if the records show a lien, an old foreclosure or an unknown heir?

The title company searches these records ahead of closing, which is when loose ends appear. Typical finds include a mortgage paid off with no release on file, a hospital lien, a mechanic's lien, or a deed signed by a relative who has died.

  • Unpaid property tax stays with the house. The county's tax office calls taxes delinquent if unpaid before February 1 of the next year, and its tax sales run online through GovEase.
  • The trustee named on each notice conducts a foreclosure sale, and the clerk does not. Sales are held on the outside steps at the 2nd floor entrance of the courthouse at 501 Washington Ave., usually starting at 10:00 a.m., and the notices can be read at the clerk's office.
  • An inherited house can be sorted out through probate, and the County Clerk keeps those case files. An affidavit of heirship can also be recorded with the clerk, though the State Law Library points out that no law makes anyone accept it.

When a record problem is holding up a sale, a buyer who purchases as-is and works through the title company may handle the cleanup as part of closing.

Who appraises McLennan County property, and when is a protest due?

Values for county tax purposes come from the McLennan Central Appraisal District at 315 S 26th Street, Waco. A spring Notice of Appraised Value goes to owners whose market value rose by at least $1,000, and the district puts the protest deadline at May 15 or 30 days after mailing, whichever falls later.

A filed protest first gets an informal meeting with an appraiser, and an unsettled case moves to the Appraisal Review Board. Online protests for most residential property run April 10 through May 15, per the district. Homestead exemptions use Form 50-114 and are generally due by April 30.

The deed index does not show the tax bill, so a buyer should ask the McLennan County Tax Office for the account status. A tax lien attaches each January 1, and the owner that day answers for that year.

How large is McLennan County?

The Census Bureau put McLennan County at 272,020 people as of July 1, 2025, compared with 260,579 in the 2020 census and 234,906 in 2010. The county has 1,036.66 square miles of land and held 251.4 people a mile in 2020.

For 2020 through 2024, 61.8% of homes were lived in by their owners, and the midpoint home value was $243,600. Gross rent at the midpoint was $1,173 and household income at the midpoint was $66,643, across 97,338 households of about 2.64 people. The Bureau also lists 1,442 building permits for 2025 and 112,290 housing units in mid-2025.

Have the title company compare the recorded deed, the tax account and the seller's name early, so a mismatch surfaces well before closing.

More questions about McLennan County, TX Property Records

Is there a way to find a McLennan County deed from a street address?

No. Records are indexed by name, not legal description, so you need the grantor or grantee. Online Records Search handles 1996 onward, and the Records Building workstations handle older volumes.

Where is the McLennan County Clerk's office?

Room 223 of the McLennan County Records Building, 215 N 5th Street, Waco, TX 76701, telephone 254-757-5078, open weekdays from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. except holidays.

Can the clerk's office notarize my deed?

No notary works at the counter, per the clerk's FAQ. Sign in front of a notary elsewhere and bring the original, because copies are not accepted.

Does the County Clerk run the foreclosure sale?

No, the trustee named on each notice runs it. Sales happen on the courthouse steps at 501 Washington Ave., Waco, and notices are available at the clerk's office.

How do I find out whether back taxes are owed on a McLennan County house?

Ask the McLennan County Tax Office, which treats a bill as delinquent when unpaid before February 1 of the next year. The title company's commitment will show unpaid tax as well.

Clay County property records FAQ

Where do I search Clay County property records?

Start with the county clerk's office. We did not confirm an online search for this county.

Can I search Clay County property records online?

Not at this time, according to the clerk. The Clay County Clerk's page says deed records are digitized back to the 1960s and that property records are currently not available online. Plan to call or visit the clerk's office in Henrietta, and ask for the record by owner name, legal description or instrument number.

The clerk's page adds two limits owners should know. The clerk cannot give legal advice or services, and the clerk has no duty to search public records, citing Attorney General opinion WW-607. A title company or attorney does the searching.

Where is the Clay County Clerk's office and when is it open?

The office is in the Courthouse Annex at 214 N. Main Street, Henrietta, TX 76365, with a mailing address of P.O. Box 548. The phone is (940) 538-4631 and the fax is (940) 264-4160. Hours are Monday to Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., and the annex closes from noon to 1:00 p.m. every day.

  • The office closes for major holidays.
  • It may close for court hearings, training or bad weather, so call before a long drive.
  • Historic Commissioners' Court record books from the 1870s have been restored and are kept in the clerk's office.

What ID do I need to file a deed in Clay County?

A government photo ID. A notice posted by the clerk explains that Senate Bill 16, effective September 1, 2025, adds Local Government Code 191.010(b): the clerk must require photo ID from whoever presents a document for the real property records, must copy it, and must reject the filing if the person refuses.

The notice describes the law as a statewide deed fraud measure. It also tightens criminal penalties for real property theft and fraud, lets victims seek restitution and a no-fee judicial voiding of a fraudulent deed, and sets stronger standards for notaries. A seller who plans to mail a deed should ask the clerk how the ID rule applies to documents delivered by a title company.

What does the Clay County Clerk charge to record a deed?

The first page costs $25 in total, and each added page costs $4, based on the clerk's fee schedule effective September 1, 2025. Other recording lines from that schedule are below.

Clay County Clerk recording fees as printed in the schedule effective September 1, 2025

The $25 first-page figure is built from a $10 archive fee, a $5 recording fee and a $10 records management fee. Each name to be indexed beyond five adds $0.25.

What mistakes make the Clay County Clerk charge extra or refuse a deed?

Format errors raise the price or stop the filing, and the schedule lists them:

  • No grantee mailing address on a deed signed after December 31, 1981 brings a penalty equal to the greater of twice the filing fee or $25, on top of regular fees.
  • No clear heading at the top of the first page doubles the filing fee for that page.
  • Names not legibly typed or printed under each signature double the fee for that page.
  • Printed type must be no smaller than 8 point, per the schedule's citation of Local Government Code 191.007.
  • The deed needs original signatures and a proper acknowledgment under Property Code 12.001(b).

Copies cost $1.00 per page, certification is $5.00 per document, and a notice of trustee sale carries a $2.00 fee. A returned check costs $30.

Which state recording rules sit behind Clay County's fee schedule?

The Texas county clerk manual describes the clerk as the county recorder, with deed records filed in the county where the land lies. It lists the instruments a clerk records, among them general and special warranty deeds, quitclaim deeds, trustee's deeds, sheriff's deeds, tax deeds, deed of trust releases and powers of attorney. The manual also lets a commissioners court tell the clerk to waive real property recording fees for buyers using certain federal or state grant programs. Ask the Henrietta office whether that option has been adopted.

How do probate and heirs affect a Clay County house sale?

If an owner has died, a probate filing may be needed before the house can be sold. The County Clerk's fee schedule lists a base probate or guardianship filing at $360, and $418 when a citation is issued and posted by the sheriff. A will left for safekeeping with the clerk costs $16. The clerk's page also links a guardianship registration form and civil court cost instructions.

Ask the clerk or a Texas attorney which route fits a particular estate. County clerks cannot advise on that choice, as the clerk's page states plainly.

What does the Clay Appraisal District handle?

Value and exemptions, but not tax collection. The Clay County Appraisal District FAQ says it does not levy taxes, set rates or collect them, and that you must call the proper tax office for amounts. Its site, claycad.org, carries forms, an interactive map, protest hearing information and an oil and gas FAQ.

  • Homestead exemption: you must have owned and lived in the home on January 1, and it must be your principal residence. The district says the claim covers up to 20 acres of residential land.
  • Filing window: January 1 to April 30 of the tax year, with a late homestead claim allowed up to two years after taxes become delinquent.
  • Over 65: the claim can be filed up to one year after the 65th birthday, with proof of age.
  • Mobile homes can be set up as improvement-only accounts if you file a request for separate taxation with the title or a verified purchase contract.

The Comptroller calendar gives May 15, or the 30th day after notice is delivered when later, as the usual protest deadline. The CAD FAQ adds that a protest letter need not be on an official form.

What do the Census figures say about Clay County?

Clay is a thinly settled county. Census QuickFacts reports a July 2025 estimate of 10,764 people, up from 10,218 at the 2020 census, on 1,088.76 square miles. That works out to 9.4 people per square mile in 2020.

  • Housing units: 5,247, with only 8 building permits in 2025
  • Owner-occupied rate: 84.0%, across 4,289 households
  • Median owner-occupied home value: $171,500 for 2020 to 2024
  • Median gross rent: $811; median household income: $80,114
  • Residents 65 or older: 24.7%

With so few sales, a comparable house may be miles away. Ask a title company for recent recorded deed prices in your part of the county.

More questions about Clay County, TX Property Records

Are Clay County property records available online?

No. The Clay County Clerk's page says deed records are digitized back to the 1960s but that property records are currently not available online. Call (940) 538-4631 or visit the annex in Henrietta.

What are the hours of the Clay County Clerk?

Monday to Friday, 7:30 a.m. to 4:00 p.m., with the annex closed from noon to 1:00 p.m. daily. The office may close for hearings, training or bad weather.

Do I need a photo ID to record a deed in Clay County?

Yes. Under Local Government Code 191.010(b), added by Senate Bill 16 effective September 1, 2025, the clerk must require photo ID from the person presenting a real property document, copy it and reject the filing if the person refuses.

How much does it cost to record a deed in Clay County?

The clerk's schedule effective September 1, 2025 lists $25 for the first page and $4 for each added page. Missing grantee addresses, a missing heading or unreadable printed names add penalties.

Who collects property tax in Clay County?

Not the appraisal district. The Clay CAD says it does not collect taxes, so call the proper tax office for amounts. The appraisal district's site lists a separate Pay Taxes Online link for that purpose.

Ownership and value in King County

Where do I find and record property records in King County, Texas?

Deeds and other land papers for King County are recorded by the County Clerk in Guthrie, and the clerk's web page links to an online records search. Walk-in visitors go to 800 South Baker; mail goes to P.O. Box 135, Guthrie, TX 79236. The telephone number is 806.596.4412 and the fax is 806.596.4664.

The clerk's page asks people who send a document by mail to include a self-addressed envelope for its return. No fee total is printed beside that request, and hours are not posted, so phone the office before you put a check in the mail.

  • The original deed with ink signatures and the notary's acknowledgment
  • A mailing address for every grantee, since leaving it off can trigger an extra charge
  • An envelope addressed to yourself with postage on it
  • A check for whatever amount the clerk quotes

Which King County offices handle which part of a property file?

Three offices in Guthrie split the work on any parcel. The clerk keeps recorded documents, the chief appraiser keeps value and exemption files, and the tax assessor-collector sends statements and takes payments. Each lists its own post office box on the county website.

The appraisal office also posts board meeting notices on its county page, which helps if you want to know when the board that oversees valuations next meets.

What must a deed show before the King County Clerk will record it?

Texas will not let a clerk record a land conveyance unless the signature was acknowledged, or sworn before two witnesses (Property Code 12.001(b)). The 2023 county clerk manual lists what goes into the deed records: warranty deeds of both kinds, quitclaims, trustee's, sheriff's and tax deeds, releases of liens, leases, powers of attorney and several affidavits.

That manual also explains how the bill is built. Page one carries $5.00 and each added page $4.00 under Local Government Code 118.012, and records management, archive and technology charges come on top within statutory caps. Because each county picks its own add-ons, the King County total will differ from the base numbers, so ask the office for the whole amount.

Land records follow the land. A deed for a King County house goes to Guthrie, wherever the seller now lives, whether that is Lubbock, Wichita Falls or another state.

What kind of county is King County, Texas?

King County is among the smallest counties in the nation by population. Census Bureau figures show about 192 people for mid-2025, against 265 in the 2020 count and 286 in 2010. Its 910.87 square miles of land hold roughly 0.3 people per square mile.

The Handbook of Texas places the county in the Rolling Prairie region of northwest Texas, with Cottle, Foard, Knox, Stonewall and Dickens counties around it. The legislature created it on August 21, 1876, and it was organized in 1891 with Guthrie as county seat. Big ranches drove its early story: the Four Sixes, the Pitchfork, the Matador and the SMS. Oil came in 1943, and beef cattle remain the main farm product. U.S. 83 runs north and south, U.S. 82 east and west, and Dumont and Finney are the other named communities. The handbook calls Guthrie, with about 160 people when the entry was written, the largest town and the seat of government, which is why county records business all lands in that one town.

Survey years 2020 through 2024 count 111 households averaging 1.90 people, and the estimate for housing units is 177. Owners live in 59.5 percent of homes, a middle-priced owned home is worth $52,100, and nearly one in four people, 22.9 percent, is 65 or older.

What record problems come up when selling a house in King County?

Three snags recur: an owner who died before title was cleared, a lien nobody released, and a tax bill left unpaid. The clerk's recorded documents and the tax office files show each one, and Texas has a defined fix for each.

  • Owner died, no probate. A will may be probated within four years of death. A small estate affidavit fits only when there was no will, the assets (not counting homestead and exempt property) total $75,000 or less, and all heirs agree. A court must approve it.
  • Heirship by affidavit. A sworn heirship statement filed with the clerk is possible, yet no law forces a lender or title insurer to accept it.
  • Old mortgage. A paid-off lender should sign a release, which the clerk records like any other instrument. Request one if the payoff happened years ago.
  • Ranch or oil acreage. When a house sits on part of a larger tract, have the title agent trace whether earlier deeds reserved minerals.

Closing agents run the lien, judgment and heir searches before funds move, so these items surface early.

How do King County property taxes fit into a sale?

King County bills come from local taxing units, since the state levies no property tax of its own. The appraisal district prices each parcel using its January 1 status, and spring notices from the chief appraiser start the protest clock: file by May 15, or by the 30th day after the notice reaches you if that date falls later. Appeals past the review board can go to district court or binding arbitration.

Statements go out about October 1 with payment due by January 31. On February 1 an unpaid bill turns delinquent and picks up six percent in penalty plus one percent interest. The lien for each year's tax attaches on January 1, which means the title cannot be fully clear while a prior year remains open. The King County Tax Assessor-Collector can quote what a particular parcel owes.

For rates and exemptions, see our King County property tax guide.

How can a cash sale work when the King County records are messy?

An as-is cash purchase can still close when the deed history needs cleanup, because the title agent handles the paperwork instead of the seller doing repairs and showings. Tell us what you found in the records, such as a missing heir or an old lien, and we will explain how a sale could move forward.

The closing documents are recorded with the King County Clerk afterward. The title agent confirms payoff figures on any recorded mortgage and collects taxes due at the table.

Who records deeds in King County, Texas?

The King County Clerk in Guthrie does. Texas makes the county clerk the county recorder, so every deed for a King County house is filed at that single office.

Can I send a deed to the King County Clerk by mail?

Yes, as long as you add a self-addressed envelope, which the clerk's page asks for. Phone 806.596.4412 to get the fee, then mail the original signed and acknowledged deed showing a grantee mailing address.

Where do I dispute my King County appraisal?

Begin with the chief appraiser at P.O. Box 117 in Guthrie. A written protest to the appraisal review board is due May 15 or by the 30th day after the notice is delivered, whichever comes later.

What if the owner of a King County house died without probate?

Several routes exist: probating a will inside four years, a small estate affidavit for modest estates, a muniment of title, or an affidavit of heirship. The right one depends on whether a will exists and who the heirs are.
